To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a PCA-based linear discriminants analysis identified a 53 gene profile characteristic of transformed cells, and (2) a comparison of differential gene expression amongst all tumor types, using a MANOVA, identified 12 differentially expressed genes including ANGPTL-4, COL1-A1, GP2 (urokinase), LAMB-3, PCDH-B9, and PTGER-3.

a comparison of the expression of 3531 secretory and cell surface genes in 5 transformed cell lines and 5 derivative xenografts revealed a 12-gene profile that was characteristic of all tumors and included late angiogenic genes such as ANGTPL4 and COL1.
we have identified 7 differentially expressed genes that may be important for tumorigenesis and that these genes are associated with late angiogenic processes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of human tumors and their derived xenografts.
the expression of secreted and membrane proteins in cancer and their possible role as therapeutic targets.
the expression profiles of secreted and membrane-associated genes of transformed cells, and the use of these genes as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets in human cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the expression of a subset of the genes identified in this study are associated with the late stages of tumor development and progression.
the 7 common differential genes (ANGPTL4, ANGPTL2, COL1A2, COL1a1, PCDHB6, PCDHB7 and PCDHB8) may be involved in the process of tumorigenecity.
a combination of PCA and MANOVA is a powerful tool to identify common tumorigenesis genes in diverse cell lines and their xenograft tumors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most important common tumorigenic genes identified were those that are associated with late angiogenesis, morphogenesis and extracellular matrix formation.
the genes that we have identified in our study are likely involved in tumor growth, metastasis and angiogenesis.
the common genes identified by our study are likely involved in late angiogenic and morphogenic processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a xenografted tumor model using diverse transformed human cell lines is a good model to identify common tumorigenically important genes that may be important for tumor progression, angiogenesis and invasion.
the use of multiple cell lines of distinct tissue origin in the xenograft model is a powerful tool to identify common tumorigenesis-associated cell surface and secreted molecules.
a combination of different analyses is required to identify the most important genes that are differentially expressed in a set of tumors.
